title: Pixel-art tennis club diorama on a floating island
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Make a pixel-art 3D diorama of a small tennis club on a floating island, the same series and engine as my other pixel dioramas (three.js, orthographic isometric camera turned in quarter steps, a small render target with no anti-aliasing snapped to whole pixels, depth-based outlines, a fixed 64-colour palette matched in OKLab, hard sun shadows, day/dusk/night, rain with puddle reflections). Call it "Love All".

The club: one court inside a chain-link fence with low dark-green windscreens reading LOVE ALL, a net that sags from 1.07 m at the posts to 0.914 m at the strap, the umpire's high chair with a sunshade and the players' chairs with parasols, a three-row stand, a clubhouse with a red roof, a clock showing the real time, a flag and a terrace, a groundsman's shed, floodlights (spotlights aimed at the court, so night stays dark around it), poplars and a gravel path. The court can be clay, grass or a hard court, painted to the rule book.

Real ball physics: gravity, drag and the Magnus force of topspin and slice; a different bounce on each surface; net cords that trickle over or drop back. Players predict the ball's flight, pick where the strings can meet it (after the bounce, or on the volley or smash at the net), run there and swing in time. Each figure is a rig of boxes posed with two-bone IK; the racket follows keyed paths for a forehand, a two-handed backhand, a volley, a smash and a serve with toss, trophy pose and jump, and the strings meet the ball at contact. Shot choice comes from the situation (cross court, down the line, sharp angle, slice when stretched, lob or pass against a net rusher, drop shot against a deep player, approach and volley). Each launch is solved to clear the net and land on its target, then thrown a little off, so winners, errors and long rallies come out of the physics. Four players with their own styles play a ladder where the winner stays on: short sets to four games, no-ad scoring, a tiebreak at 3–3 and a match tiebreak to ten.

Life on court: ball kids fetch dead balls and bounce a new one to the server, who bounces it before serving. The umpire watches the ball and calls the score. On clay the ball leaves marks, and on close calls the umpire climbs down to read the mark. Between sets the groundsmen drag the clay; grass wears behind the baselines. In rain the players sit under their parasols and the groundsmen pull a cover over the court. Spectators follow the ball and clap. Click the court to aim the next shot, with buttons for a lob or a drop shot, and a ×3 speed toggle. Show a tennis scoreboard (sets, point, server, serve speed) and the ladder; English UI; it must work on phones.

title: Interactive Lamborghini FL3 tractor diesel engine
author: exploraX_
prompt:
Build an interactive 3D web page: a live "bench study" of the **Lamborghini FL3**, the air-cooled three-cylinder diesel that powered the Lamborghini 2R tractor (1961 to 1967), from the years before Lamborghini built cars. Visitors should be able to start the engine, rev it, load it, cut it open, watch the cooling air, and take it apart. The page should feel like a beautifully printed technical plate that happens to be alive.

## Hard rules

- **Everything procedural.** No 3D models, no Blender, no textures, no image files, no audio files. Geometry, materials, drawings and sound are all generated in code.
- **three.js (WebGL)**, vendored locally, ES modules with an importmap, no build step. It must run from a plain static server.
- **60 fps** on a recent laptop at 1440x900 and on a retina display.
- **Desktop:** the whole sheet fits a 1440x900 viewport with no scrolling.
- **Phone width:** the sheet becomes a vertical scroll with nothing cut off. On touch, horizontal drags turn the engine and vertical swipes scroll the page.
- **No em dashes** anywhere in the copy.

## The engine: facts

Only these figures are published. Use them exactly:

- 3 cylinders, inline, air-cooled, direct-injection diesel, Lamborghini type FL3
- bore 92 mm, stroke 110 mm, 2,193 cc
- 39 hp (29.1 kW) at 2,200 rpm
- electric starter, Bosch injection
- about 2,000 2Rs sold between 1961 and 1967
- factory colours: orange and light blue ("celeste")

The external layout, from photographs of a restored 1962 2R:

- the engine block painted celeste
- an axial cooling blower in a round housing at the front, belt-driven from the crank, with a wire guard
- a sheet-metal air cowl along the cold side
- individual finned cylinder barrels and finned heads, held down by long studs
- a silver inline injection pump on the hot side, with three copper high-pressure lines up to the injectors
- twin fuel filters
- a black vertical exhaust stack with a silencer and a flapper rain cap
- an oil-bath air cleaner
- a dynamo, a starter motor, and a flywheel with a ring gear

Everything else is an assumption and must be labelled **modelled** on the page:

- compression ratio (about 17:1), rod length, valve timing
- idle (about 700 rpm) and high idle (about 2,350 rpm)
- torque curve, friction, airflow, temperatures, fuel use

Never dimension an assumed size in the drawings.

## Art direction: a 1960s Italian two-ink print

It must not look like a Victorian parchment plate or a generic blueprint. Think of a page from an Italian factory manual or a mid-century industrial catalogue, printed in the tractor's own two inks.

- **Paper:** ivory offset stock (about #EEE9DC) with fine paper grain and soft, uneven ink absorption.
- **Inks:** arancio (#E0561C), celeste (#58AED6 for the print, a deeper #3F9DD0 for the painted engine) and near-black (#1C1B19).
- **Type:**
- Bodoni Moda for display: a huge "FL3" with the 3 in arancio, and an italic "Lamborghini" above it.
- Archivo for labels (wide, letter-spaced small caps).
- IBM Plex Mono for numbers.
- Every label carries its Italian term in small italic Bodoni (for example: Hand throttle *acceleratore*).
- **Print details:**
- registration marks in the four corners and a colour bar in the margin
- a thin double frame and a running head across the top: "Bench study · *banco prova*", "Air-cooled diesel · three cylinders · direct injection", "Sheet 03"
- a giant celeste numeral "3" printed faintly behind the engine, slightly out of register
- **Layout at 1440x900:**
- left column: title, deck, lede and the controls
- centre: the 3D engine
- right column: four live instruments
- bottom strip: four live drawings and a readings card

Copy:
- Kicker: "Lamborghini Trattori · 1961–1967"
- Deck: "Three cylinders. No radiator."
- Lede: "Before the supercars, Lamborghini built tractors. The 2R of 1961 carried this engine: 2,193 cc of direct-injection diesel and no radiator, cooled by a belt-driven blower and cast fins. About 2,000 were sold by 1967, and tractor money paid for the move into cars in 1963."

## The 3D model

Build the FL3 to its real proportions: 92 mm bore, 110 mm stroke, cylinders about 150 mm apart, crank axis as the origin.

Exterior parts:

- crankcase with main-bearing ribs and mounting feet, oil sump, timing case, flywheel plate
- three separate finned barrels, with the fins flattened where neighbours meet
- three finned heads with rocker covers and long studs
- blower with a spinning rotor, stator vanes and a guard
- V-belt around the crank, dynamo and blower pulleys
- air cowl with a stencilled "FL3 · raffreddato ad aria"
- intake runners into the oil-bath air cleaner with a glass pre-cleaner bowl
- exhaust manifold, silencer and a flapper cap that lifts on each exhaust pulse at idle
- injection pump with a governor housing whose throttle lever follows the hand throttle
- copper injector lines and a leak-off line, injectors, twin fuel filters
- starter motor whose pinion slides into the ring gear while cranking
- a small name plate reading "MOTORE DIESEL · FL3 · CV 39 · 2200 g/min" (no company logo anywhere)

Moving internals:

- crankshaft with counterweights, pins 120 degrees apart, turning clockwise seen from the blower end
- connecting rods, pistons with rings and a combustion bowl
- camshaft at half speed with lobes timed to the valve events
- tappets, pushrods, rockers, valves and springs that compress, all driven by the same valve-lift curves the simulation uses

Materials and setting:

- **Materials:** glossy celeste enamel with subtle procedural grain, rougher on castings than on sheet metal. Steel, alloy, copper and heat-darkened exhaust.
- **Stand:** the engine sits on an **arancio test stand**.
- **Lighting and floor:** a soft cast shadow and a contact shadow lands on the paper itself (a transparent canvas over the page).
- **Life at rest:** the engine rocks slightly on its mounts against the gas torque.

## The simulation

Write it as a pure, testable module.

- **Kinematics:**
- exact slider-crank piston motion and rod angle
- four-stroke cycle over 720 degrees, firing order 1-2-3, one firing every 240 degrees
- **In-cylinder pressure:**
- polytropic compression and expansion with a double-Wiebe heat release (fast premixed burn plus a slower diffusion burn), tabulated by fuel level
- calibrate the heat release so that full fuel at 2,200 rpm gives exactly 29.1 kW at the flywheel
- peak pressure lands around 70 to 75 bar at full load
- **Crank dynamics:**
- integrate with sub-steps of about 2 degrees of crank, so the instantaneous gas torque gives real speed ripple at idle and real compression pulses while cranking
- flywheel inertia about 0.8 kg·m²
- **Governor and load:**
- an all-speed mechanical governor with about 120 rpm of droop and a little fuel-rack lag
- the hand throttle sets the governed speed between idle and high idle
- the PTO brake applies a load that rises with the square of speed, so 100% load at 2,200 rpm needs exactly full fuel
- **Starting:**
- the starter cranks at about 250 rpm
- the charge needs a few compressions before it lights, the first cycles misfire and burn rich, and that black smoke leaves the stack
- the engine catches in about 1 second and the starter disengages
- **Stopping:**
- friction rises with speed, plus blower drag rising with the square of speed
- an unfired cylinder gives back less than it took to compress (heat lost to the fins), so the engine stops about 2 seconds after the fuel is cut at idle
- **Temperatures:**
- head temperatures come from about a quarter of the fuel's heat going into the metal, removed by blower air that rises with engine speed
- full load settles around 160 to 175 °C
- run thermal time 30 times faster than real time and say so

The simulation emits events with timestamps: crank, fire, misfire, exhaust valve opening, caught, stop, stalled. Events raised between steps (the key) must not be lost.

## Interaction

- **Ignition key:** a round bakelite-and-steel switch. Click (or Space) to start and stop. It shows Start, Cranking or Stop.
- **Two levers:** the hand throttle shows the governed rpm, and the PTO brake shows a percentage. Style them as notched quadrants with orange lever knobs.
- **Four views** (keys 1 to 4), each with a smooth scripted camera move:
- **Painted.**
- **Cutaway:**
- a section plane through the cylinder axes, with cut faces printed as a light arancio hatch
- parts lying wholly in the removed half (pump, filters, exhaust, starter, pushrods, cam) disappear
- pistons, rods and crank stay whole
- a combustion glow fills each chamber as it fires
- **Airflow:**
- everything except the barrels and heads fades to a paper-grey ghost
- barrels and heads show a temperature ramp from deep celeste to arancio
- particles are drawn in through the blower guard, run along the cowl, cross the fins and leave warm on the pump side
- particles are drawn through the metal like the flow arrows of a technical illustration
- **Exploded:**
- waits until the engine has stopped, then separates the parts along sensible axes and holds the crank still
- each part gets a callout: English name in small caps, Italian term in italic, and a leader line to an orange dot
- labels sit on a paper backing and never overlap
- **Other controls:**
- Slow motion (S) eases time to 1/25
- a Sound toggle
- Reset view
- drag to orbit, scroll to zoom
- **Narration line:** a single italic line in the console that reacts to what is happening. Examples:
- "Key turned. The starter pinion meshes with the flywheel and spins the engine at about 250 rpm."
- "Squeezed about 17 to 1, the air gets hot enough to light the diesel. No spark plugs."
- "It caught."
- "Idling near 700 rpm: three power strokes every two turns, one every 240 degrees."
- "The hand throttle sets the governor, which opens the rack until the engine holds that speed."
- "Full PTO load at 2,200 rpm: the rack is wide open and the FL3 makes its rated 39 hp."
- "No water anywhere. The blower pushes air down the cowl, across the fins, and out warm on the pump side."
- "Fuel cut. It runs down and rocks back on its last compression."
- Each view also gets a line of its own.

## Live instruments (Canvas 2D, ink on paper)

1. **Tachometer:** a period Italian dial, 0 to 25 x100 rpm, with an arancio arc above rated speed and an hour meter whose tenths drum rolls.
2. **The cycle:** a 720-degree wheel with three rings (one per cylinder, offset 240 degrees). Power is arancio, exhaust grey, intake celeste, compression hatched. A pointer follows the crank and a dot flashes at each firing.
3. **Indicator diagram:** the live P-V loop for cylinder 1, with the full-load loop dashed for reference, a dot at the current state and the peak pressure labelled.
4. **Chart recorder:** scrolling chart paper with an rpm pen in black and a power pen in arancio.

Below the drawings, a **readings card**:

- live values: speed, power, torque, fuel (l/h), cooling air (m³/min) and head temperature
- marked "live, modelled"
- a footnote listing what is published and stating that the page is an independent study, not affiliated with Lamborghini

Power and torque are measured at the flywheel, so they never overshoot the rated 39 hp during transients.

## Live drawings: blueline prints of the running engine

Front, Right side, Plan and **Section A-A** are real orthographic renders of the same running model, not illustrations. Ink them in a shader like 1960s diazo prints:

- render normals and depth, then draw blue outlines from silhouette, crease and depth edges
- shade with a celeste 45-degree screentone
- print an arancio hatch wherever the section plane cuts metal
- the diazo paper and its faint grid are printed by the shader itself
- add centre lines and numbered cylinders
- Section A-A cuts through cylinder 1 so you see the piston moving. It dimensions only the published bore (Ø 92) and stroke (110), with TDC and BDC lines marked PMS and PMI.

## Sound (Web Audio, synthesised)

- **Exhaust:** each pop is scheduled from the simulation's own exhaust-valve events at the correct sub-frame time. It is not a looped sample.
- **Layers:**
- diesel knock at each injection
- blower roar and a blade-pass tone tracking speed
- valve-gear whirr
- a starter whine that strains on each compression
- a solenoid clunk on start and stop
- the flapper cap ticking at idle
- a soft metallic cue when the engine comes apart and a seating clunk when it goes back together
- **Slow motion** spaces the pops out and deepens them.
- **Mix:** run everything through a compressor. It must never clip.
- **Autoplay:** audio starts on the first user gesture.

## Deliverables

- the page: `index.html`, `css/`, `js/`, with three.js vendored in `vendor/`
- a tiny no-cache static server (`https://serve.py/`)
- a README that separates published facts from modelled ones
- a headless Node check of the simulation that asserts:
- 29.1 kW at 2,200 rpm
- peak pressure 60 to 85 bar
- catches within 3 s
- idles between 650 and 750 rpm
- full load holds about 2,200 rpm and 39 hp
- heads pass 120 °C under load
- it stops after the fuel is cut
- optional: a frame-exact video capture script (virtual time at 60 fps, a drawn cursor with click rings, the sound rendered offline from the simulation's event log so it stays in sync)

## Done means

1. The sheet loads with no console errors and holds 60 fps.
2. Turning the key cranks, catches with a dark puff and settles near 700 rpm.
3. Full throttle plus full PTO load reads about 2,200 rpm and 39 hp, and the P-V loop peaks around 73 bar.
4. Every view works, including Section A-A cutting through the moving piston.
5. The exploded view waits for the engine to stop, and its labels are all readable.
6. Every figure that is not published is labelled as modelled.
7. At 1440x900 nothing overflows, and at phone width nothing is cut off.

title: Jelly cube spaceport comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build "Launch Jelly" — a single-file interactive WebGPU diorama in the "Material Studies" series: a spaceport on a low tropical island, cut out as a cube of translucent jelly on a studio floor. Everything procedural (no external assets, no network), one HTML file with inline JS/WGSL.

THE BLOCK
- A wobbly jelly cube you can grab by its sides and tip; it springs back. Sliders: firmness, wave damping, wind (0–20 m/s).
- Shallow-water sim for the sea (wind waves, wakes, foam), sandy seabed with ripples and caustics, seagrass, coral heads, sponges, starfish, conchs, an old rocket engine bell on the bottom. Cut faces show sand, shelly limestone and candy strata. Drag the water to stir it.

THE SCENE
- Land along the back and left: dunes, scrub, palms, dune grass, a beach.
- Launch pad on a concrete berm: mount over a flame trench opening toward the sea, steel deflector, four red-and-white lightning masts with sagging catenary wires, a deluge water tower, tank farm (LOX sphere, kerosene tanks, nitrogen bottles), floodlights.
- A long hangar with ribbed siding and a vertical-lift door, rails to the pad, a transporter-erector (white lattice strongback on a rail car with hydraulic rams).
- Landing zone (concrete circle with ring and cross), refurbishment shed, fire truck, a tracking radar dish that follows whatever is flying.
- Press site: bleachers full of spectators, a flag, a big amber seven-segment countdown clock (T−0:10 … T+0:45).
- Quay with fenders and bollards, a crawler crane with a long lattice boom, two booster stands, a warehouse.
- At sea: a drone ship (dark deck with landing target, blast walls, thruster houses), a tug, a fairing-recovery boat with a big net on four arms.
- The rocket: two stages — booster with nine engines, black interstage, four folding landing legs, four grid fins; upper stage with a long dark vacuum nozzle; a two-piece fairing whose halves carry parafoils.

WHAT HAPPENS
- Roll out: the hangar door lifts, the erector carries the rocket out horizontally on rails and stands it on the mount; it vents LOX wisps.
- Launch: 10-second count with beeps and the clock, strongback leans back, deluge water, ignition at T−3 with huge steam clouds boiling out of the trench toward the sea, slow liftoff, the block trembles, the crowd cheers, gulls go up. The rocket pitches downrange and climbs out of sight leaving a billowing exhaust trail; the camera rises with it.
- Staging: MECO, separation, the upper stage lights a pale blue-violet vacuum flame and leaves. The booster flips, boostback burn, grid fins out, entry burn, steers down, landing burn on one engine, legs swing out, touchdown — on the drone ship or back at the landing zone (toggle, or tap the ship / the pad). Double sonic boom (triple for the landing zone). Boosters come back sooty; the deck and pad get scorched.
- Recovery: the tug tows the drone ship to the quay; the crane hooks the booster, lifts it (pendulum swing), folds its legs, sets it on a stand; the ship is towed back out. Fairing halves come down under orange-and-white parafoils, circling in: one lands in the boat's net, the other splashes and is fished out; the boat brings them home.
- Reuse: the next rollout takes a flight-proven booster ("B1 · flight 2", soot partly cleaned).
- Storm: wind, waves, rain, darkened room, lightning on the masts, the crane or the sea. No launches in a storm or above 15 m/s ("No go · weather / wind"); a count in progress holds.

LIFE
- Brown pelicans that circle and plunge-dive for fish, gulls on masts, lamps and roofs, a pod of bottlenose dolphins, manatees grazing the shallows and surfacing to breathe, fish schools, moon jellies; pad crew who leave before the count, hands on the quay, spectators who raise their arms at liftoff and landing.

RENDERING
- Engine plumes as glowing translucent cones (white-hot core, orange, shock diamonds low down, widening and turning blue-violet in thin air) that light the ground, the smoke and the rocket orange; steam and exhaust as soft lit puffs; soot streaks on flown boosters; shadows, refraction, caustics.

CONTROLS & UI
- Buttons: Roll out, Launch (Hold during the count), Land on ship / Land at pad, Storm. Space rolls out / launches. Taps: rocket = launch, hangar = roll out, drone ship / landing zone = choose landing site.
- Tallies: Launches, Landings, Fairings; status lines for the Rocket (T−/T+ timeline: Liftoff, Max Q, Stage separation, Boostback, Entry burn, Landing burn…), the Drone ship and the Fairing boat.
- Flavours: Lime, Curaçao, Blackcurrant. Sound toggle, pause, reset, view.
- All sounds synthesised with WebAudio, only for events (door motor, hydraulics, countdown beeps, engine roar loop while burning, sonic booms, touchdown thud, tug horn, winch, net catch, thunder) — no background ambience.
- Mobile bottom sheet, touch orbit, pinch zoom; a fallback message without WebGPU.
- Copy: "Launch Jelly. A spaceport on a low island, its rockets flying and coming home, set in a block of jelly." — "Roll it out. Light it up. Bring the booster home."

title: Pixel-art 3D football yard simulation with kids and dog
author: N1njaCodex
prompt:
Build a single-page web toy called "Yard Box": a real-time 3D scene rendered as pixel art, showing a courtyard football box behind a four-storey panel apartment block on a floating island. Use three.js r160 (ES module via import map from jsDelivr, plus BufferGeometryUtils). English UI. Original design only — no real brands, places or logos.

RENDERING PIPELINE (the core look)
- Orthographic camera at an isometric angle (elevation ≈31°, azimuth π/4, rotatable in 90° steps with smooth easing; drag sideways or buttons to turn; wheel/pinch zoom 0.7–2.6).
- Render into a small WebGLRenderTarget (half-float, nearest filtering, depth texture) — about 480×300 art pixels at pixel size 3 — no anti-aliasing. Fit the island + the top of the block into the screen area left free by the UI, and snap the camera so the world origin lands on a whole art pixel (static things never shimmer).
- Post-pass ShaderMaterial: texelFetch whole-pixel upscale; depth-based outlines (a pixel > ~0.5 m in front of a neighbour darkens ×0.5); quantize every pixel to the nearest of a fixed ~60-colour palette in OKLab (lightness weighted ×1.35); optional 4×4 Bayer dither (off by default); empty depth = page background colour.
- "Raw 3D" toggle shows the full-resolution MSAA render without steps above. Controls: pixel size slider 2–6, palette / dither / outlines checkboxes.
- Palette: warm concrete greys, cool greys for snow in shade/moonlight, snow and sky blues, turf greens, autumn olives, yellows/oranges/rusts, team reds and blues, skin and wood tones, lamp/window yellows, dusk violets, mint for the boards.

LIGHT AND TIME
- Directional sun/moon with hard BasicShadowMap (2048), hemisphere fill, point lights for two streetlamps (decay 2) and weak doorway lamps. Presets Day / Dusk / Night blended over 1.6 s. Glow materials lerp between on/off colours.
- The block's facade uses an emissive map drawn on a canvas; at night windows glow warm or cool, and random flats switch lights on and off.

WORLD (all boxes, cylinders, extrusions; textures drawn texel by texel on canvases)
- Rounded floating slab: grass top over soil over rock.
- Football box: rounded-rectangle boards (22×12 m, mint green, plank lines, a gate with an open door), netting on posts above the boards at both ends, mini goals (3 m × 2 m) with alpha-tested nets, turf texture with mowing stripes, worn goalmouths/centre and white markings.
- Panel block along one long side: 4 floors, facade drawn panel by panel with windows and curtains, two entrances with canopies, random balconies, roof details; an asphalt strip with two benches and hedges.
- Dollhouse cut: when the camera looks from the block's side, hide the floors, roof, balconies and canopies and show a section of the ground floor instead — low cut walls with a dark cap, rooms with coloured floors, rugs, sofas, tables, wardrobes, TVs (glowing at night), pot plants, stairwells with steps and post boxes; room floors glow warm at night.
- Playground (swing that actually swings, slide, sandbox), birches with white trunks and dark marks, painted-tyre flower beds, a parked car, a washing line with swaying sheets, two lamp posts.

PEOPLE AND DOG
- Kids as rigs of ~17 boxes (bigger heads), posed every frame with two-bone IK: running stride, kicks keyed as back-swing → strike → follow-through, keeper stance, sideways dives, catch/hold/throw, goal celebrations (airplane arms).
- Three grandmothers sitting on the benches (cheer on goals), a small kid on the swing.
- A box-built dog that lives by the benches.

GAME LOGIC
- 3v3: two field players + one keeper per team (RED attacks +x, BLUE −x), first to 5, then a new game; scoreboard with score, game number, status line and games won.
- Kick-off from the centre; open play with dribbling by small touches, passes leading the receiver, shots aimed inside a post at random height with angular error growing with distance and pressure, tackles; players get behind the ball before kicking (feed-forward on a rolling ball), squeeze in at an angle when the ball is against the boards, avoid goal frames; a scramble poke if nobody can reach a still ball for 3.5 s.
- Keepers hold position, come out for slow loose balls, read shots after a 0.1–0.3 s reaction delay with some error, dive, catch or parry.
- Ball physics in 4 substeps: gravity, ground bounce (lower in winter), boards (lively below rail height, dead in the netting above), posts and crossbar, the goal net, legs in the way. Status flashes: GOAL!, SAVED!, WHAT A SAVE!, OFF THE POST!, OFF THE BOARDS, TACKLE.
- Every 100–170 s (or on a button) the dog runs in through the gate, grabs the ball, runs loops away from the kids for ~5 s, drops it and trots home; it gives up if the game resets.

SEASONS (Summer / Autumn / Winter)
- Summer: poplar fluff drifting. Autumn: yellow/orange canopies, leaves falling from the birches, leaf litter on the ground, olive grass. Winter: snow on the ground, roofs, benches, car and boards; bare trees; falling snow and kicked-up snow spray; kids wear hats; the ball turns orange.

INPUT AND UI
- Click the player on the ball to shoot, his teammate to pass, the pitch to make him dribble there; keys S, P, D, Space, Q/E or arrows.
- Layout: title and caption top-left, lit pixel-font scoreboard top-centre, a narrow control rail on the right (Time, Season, Game, View), a hint bottom-left, a fold-out "How it's drawn" panel bottom-right. Fonts: Silkscreen, Rubik, JetBrains Mono. Light and dark themes via CSS tokens; on phones everything stacks under the scene. WebGL2 fallback card.

title: Jelly physics simulation improvement comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Create Citrus Jelly — an interactive 3D scene featuring a gummy orange slice. Everything must run directly in the browser in a single HTML file using WebGPU and WGSL shaders. Build genuine volumetric 3D geometry, not an image or a prerecorded animation.
APPEARANCE
A thick semicircular orange slice with vibrant orange flesh, a pale pith layer, and a firmer outer rind.

Visible radial segments, thin internal membranes, and tiny bubbles.
A juicy, translucent gummy material with soft highlights, light refraction, and depth-dependent color.
Avoid making it look like rigid plastic or glass.
Use a light cream background, soft studio lighting, and a contact shadow. Avoid overexposure.
PHYSICS AND INTERACTION

Let users grab any visible point with a mouse or finger and pull it.

Deformation must originate at the grab point and propagate naturally through neighboring areas.
The flesh should stretch and narrow under tension, while the rind offers more resistance.
On release, the slice should spring back gently, with oscillations gradually settling.
Use a stable soft-body simulation: a spring mesh or volumetric elastic constraints with volume preservation.
Segments, membranes, and bubbles must deform with the flesh rather than separating or floating independently.
Include ground collisions: the slice should squash slightly on impact and wobble afterward.
Prevent instant snapping back, endless oscillation, and exploding geometry.
INTERFACE

A minimal editorial layout with generous whitespace.

A large italic serif heading, “Citrus Jelly.”, on the left.
A compact control panel on the right with Firmness and Internal damping sliders.
Give it a nudge, Reset, and Pause buttons.
Show mesh and ¼ speed toggles.
Three color presets: Orange, Blood Orange, and Lemon.
A small interaction hint: “Grab. Stretch. Let go.”
All labels in English, with comfortable desktop and mobile controls.
TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS

Genuine WebGPU rendering, not a Canvas 2D substitute.

Generate geometry and materials in code without premade models.
Use a fixed simulation timestep and constraints that prevent excessive stretching.
Maintain smooth performance during grabbing, dragging, and release.
Display a clear fallback message when WebGPU is unavailable.
Test different grab locations, strong stretching, oscillation decay, collisions, and reset.
The main priority is a convincing gummy feel. The slice should look soft, juicy, and so satisfying in motion that people want to keep stretching it.

title: Offshore jelly cube diorama comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build "Offshore Jelly" — a single-file interactive WebGPU diorama in the "Material Studies" series: a stretch of North Sea cut out as a cube of translucent jelly, sitting on a studio floor. Everything is procedural (no external assets, no network), one HTML file with inline JS/WGSL.

THE BLOCK
- A wobbly jelly cube you can grab by its sides and tip; it springs back. Sliders: firmness, damping, wind (0–20 m/s).
- Inside: a shallow-water simulation for the sea surface (waves, wakes, foam, whitecaps), seabed with sand ripples, scour rocks, kelp, boulders, starfish, crabs, urchins, a pipeline, cables and a small wreck. Caustics on the seabed. Dragging the water stirs up waves.
- Waves come from the wind: several wave trains whose height grows with wind speed.

THE SCENE
- A production platform on a four-legged steel jacket (braces, risers, conductors, boat landing, marine growth below the waterline): main and cellar decks, process module, derrick, living quarters, lifeboats, a pedestal crane with a laydown area, a flare boom with a flickering flame and smoke.
- An octagonal helideck with an H, a net, perimeter lights and a windsock.
- Five offshore wind turbines on monopiles: transition piece with yellow platform, boat landing ladder, davit, tower, nacelle, three-blade rotors with red tips, blinking red aviation lights. Rotor speed and power output (MW) follow the wind.
- A rocky skerry with a lighthouse whose beam turns; seals haul out on it.

WHAT HAPPENS
- Supply run: a platform supply vessel comes in from standby, holds station next to the jacket on dynamic positioning (thruster foam), and the crane does four lifts — containers swing on the hook, are set down on the platform and back-loaded onto the boat's deck. Then she sails back to standby.
- Helicopter: flies in from the west, turns into the wind, lands on the helideck; a deck officer walks out; passengers get off. A second press sends it away (spin-up, lift, outbound). Rotor and tail rotor spin, downwash flattens the water.
- Crew boat: a small catamaran sails out to a turbine, pushes its bow onto the boat landing, and technicians climb the ladder onto the platform. Next time she picks them up and brings them home.
- Storm: the wind builds to a gale, waves get big with whitecaps and spray, rain falls, the room darkens, lightning strikes blades, the lighthouse, the derrick or the sea with a flash and thunder. Above cut-out the turbines feather their blades and stop (0 MW); the helicopter is grounded. Then it eases and the turbines restart.

LIFE
- Schools of fish around the jacket and wrecks, gulls that perch on railings and take off on the horn, gannets that plunge-dive for fish, a pod of porpoises, seals, moon jellyfish, crew walking the decks.

CONTROLS & UI
- Buttons: Supply run, Helicopter (take-off when landed), Crew boat, Storm. Space = ship's horn. Tapping a turbine switches it on/off, tapping the supply boat or helideck calls them. Orbit by drag, zoom by wheel/pinch.
- Tallies: Power (MW), Lifts, Flights; status lines for the supply boat, helicopter and crew boat.
- Flavours (jelly colour palettes): North Sea, Curaçao, Blackcurrant.
- Sounds are synthesised with WebAudio and only play for events (horn, winch, set-down, bump, rotor, thunder, rain) — no constant background ambience. Sound toggle and pause.
- Mobile: a bottom sheet with the controls, touch orbit and pinch zoom. Clean fallback message when WebGPU is unavailable.
- Copy in English: "Offshore Jelly. A wind farm and a platform working a stretch of North Sea, set in a block of jelly." — "Call in the supply boat. Fly the crew out. Brew up a storm."

title: 'The First Spark' procedural hand-drawn short
author: morpheusdv
prompt:
PROJECT: THE FIRST SPARK — Procedural Animated Short Film

You are a senior creative coder, generative artist, animation director, and JavaScript graphics engineer.

Your task is to create a visually stunning, fully animated short film using procedural JavaScript drawing.

I have attached a reference image showing a minimalist black-ink animation on an off-white background.

Use the reference to understand the visual language, but create an original animation with its own story, composition, and movement.

Do not create a slideshow, static illustration, or simple particle demo. Build a genuine animated short film with evolving scenes, expressive character animation, cinematic transitions, and continuous visual storytelling.

1. Technical requirements

Build the project using:

JavaScript
HTML5 Canvas 2D
requestAnimationFrame for real-time playback
Procedural geometry and vector-based drawing
Bezier curves, paths, particles, and custom brush strokes
Deterministic animation based on a master timeline

All visual elements must be generated through JavaScript code.

Do not use:

AI image-generation APIs
AI video-generation APIs
External images or pre-rendered video
Stock footage
CSS-only animation
Static illustrations disguised as animation

The animation must be genuinely generated by code.

You may use lightweight JavaScript libraries if they meaningfully improve the animation, but prioritize Canvas 2D.

2. Visual direction

Create a hand-drawn, minimalist, experimental animation.

Visual characteristics:

Warm off-white paper background
Deep black ink illustrations
Slightly imperfect hand-drawn outlines
Organic brush strokes
Variable line thickness
Ink splashes and subtle paper grain
Expressive silhouette-based character design
Fluid, organic movement
Occasional dramatic camera movements
Cinematic composition

The visual result should feel like a professional independent animated short film.

Avoid generic geometric motion graphics, repetitive particle effects, and simple bouncing shapes.

Every scene should have a clear visual purpose.

3. Story: THE FIRST SPARK

Create an original 60-second animated short film.

The story follows a tiny character that emerges from a drop of black ink and gradually discovers how to create a world.

SCENE 1 — THE BEGINNING (0–8 seconds)

An empty off-white canvas.

A tiny black ink droplet appears in the center.

The droplet begins trembling.

Small irregular brush strokes emerge from it.

The ink slowly transforms into a tiny living character.

The character opens its eyes and looks around.

The camera gradually moves closer.

SCENE 2 — DISCOVERY (8–18 seconds)

The character begins walking across the empty world.

Its movement must feel alive, with animated limbs, body deformation, and subtle secondary motion.

Every step leaves behind small ink marks.

The character notices one of these marks and touches it.

The mark begins growing into an organic structure.

SCENE 3 — CREATION (18–32 seconds)

The character discovers that its movements can create new objects.

It draws a line through the air.

The line becomes a tree.

More brush strokes emerge and transform into hills, plants, and abstract structures.

The camera follows the character as the world expands.

Objects must visibly grow and transform through procedural drawing rather than suddenly appearing.

SCENE 4 — CHAOS (32–44 seconds)

The character loses control of its creation.

Black ink spreads rapidly.

The landscape becomes distorted.

Trees twist into abstract shapes.

Ink splashes fill the screen.

The camera shakes subtly as the character runs.

The animation becomes faster and more intense.

Use fluid transitions between all visual elements.

SCENE 5 — THE FIRST SPARK (44–55 seconds)

The character stops running.

Everything becomes still.

A small glowing point appears in its hand.

This is the only moment where a subtle warm accent color may be used.

The character releases the light.

The light expands into a circular wave.

The chaotic ink reorganizes into a beautiful, balanced landscape.

The camera pulls back to reveal the completed world.

SCENE 6 — ENDING (55–60 seconds)

The character stands on a small hill and looks toward the horizon.

The camera slowly moves backward.

The entire landscape gradually transforms into a single small ink drawing on the original empty canvas.

Fade to off-white.

End.

4. Animation quality requirements

This is the most important part of the project.

Every scene must contain actual animation.

The character must have:

Procedurally animated walking and running
Expressive body language
Head and body rotation
Squash and stretch
Anticipation and follow-through
Smooth transitions between poses

Environmental elements must have:

Organic growth animations
Continuous subtle movement
Non-repetitive procedural variation
Smooth transformations between shapes

Implement a virtual camera with:

Position
Zoom
Rotation
Smooth tracking
Cinematic easing

Use layered depth and camera movement to create visual richness.

Do not rely on random movement alone.

The animation should be deliberately choreographed around the story.

5. Timeline and rendering architecture

Create a centralized animation timeline.

Every visual state must be determined by the current timeline position.

Implement a function similar to:

renderFrame(time)

The function must render the correct animation frame for any requested timestamp.

Use seeded randomness so that rendering the same timestamp always produces the same image.

Do not make the animation dependent on the number of previous frames rendered.

This is essential for deterministic video export.

Target specifications:

Resolution: 1920 × 1080

Aspect ratio: 16:9

Frame rate: 30 FPS

Duration: 60 seconds

Provide an option to switch to 1080 × 1920 vertical format for social media.

6. Preview and controls

Create a local web interface that allows me to:

Play and pause the animation
Restart the animation
Scrub through the timeline
Jump between scenes
Adjust playback speed
Switch between horizontal and vertical formats
Preview the animation in real time

Display the current timestamp and scene name.

7. Video export

Implement a reliable video export workflow.

The final animation must be exportable as a high-quality MP4 file.

Use deterministic frame-by-frame rendering to avoid dropped frames or inconsistent timing.

You may use a suitable browser rendering pipeline, a frame-sequence exporter, or FFmpeg.

Do not assume that recording the browser window in real time is sufficient for production-quality export.

Provide a simple export command or interface.

8. Development process

Do not attempt to create the entire film as one enormous, untested code block.

Work in stages.

First:

Create the project architecture.
Implement the Canvas rendering engine.
Implement the deterministic timeline.
Create the character animation system.
Build Scene 1 as a fully functional visual prototype.
Run the project and inspect the visual result.

After the first scene works, continue implementing the remaining scenes.

Test the animation at multiple timestamps.

Check for rendering errors, broken transitions, inconsistent character proportions, and performance problems.

If a scene looks too simplistic, improve its procedural drawing and choreography.

9. Deliverables

Provide:

Complete JavaScript source code
Working local animation preview
Editable scene definitions
Reusable character animation system
Reusable procedural drawing functions
Video export functionality
Instructions for running the project

The final result must be a functioning animation, not just a technical demonstration.

Start by implementing the first scene and the core animation engine. Once the prototype is functional, continue with the remaining scenes.

title: 帮我做一个原创的手游「高光时刻」动效：[主体，例如：开宝箱 / 段位晋升 / 成就解锁 / Boss 掉落 / 角色升级]。…
author: op7418
prompt:
帮我做一个原创的手游「高光时刻」动效：[主体，例如：开宝箱 / 段位晋升 / 成就解锁 / Boss 掉落 / 角色升级]。
做成一个可以直接打开的单文件网页（HTML + CSS + JS），点一下就能完整播放，效果对标商业手游的结算 / 奖励演出。

【世界观与风格】
- 原创美术，不要模仿任何现有游戏的 IP、角色或 Logo。
- 卡通手游风：高饱和配色，统一的深色描边（例如 #1A1033），圆润厚重的造型。
- 配色随等级升级：[等级阶梯，例如：普通绿 → 稀有蓝 → 史诗紫 → 传说金]。每升一级都要切换主色、光效颜色和背景色调。
- 标题用圆胖的游戏字体（如 Titan One / Lilita One），描黑边，加投影；文字逐字「砸」进画面，带回弹。

【主体物：做成真 3D】
- 用 Three.js 建模，不要用平面 SVG 贴图。要有厚度、倒角，以及符合主体的结构细节（木板缝、铆钉、包边、宝石切面、锁扣等）；木板缝这类细节用真实几何体拼出来，不要贴黑线条。
- 着色用卡通分阶（MeshToonMaterial 加 3～4 阶的渐变贴图），配三种灯光：主光、天光、等级色的轮廓光。
- 描边用后期边缘检测：渲染法线图 + 深度图，再用着色器画线。外轮廓粗、零件交界细，粗细全程一致；另外做 1.5 倍超采样和多重采样抗锯齿。
  不要用「放大一圈的黑色背面」那种描边，那样粗细不均、转角会断。
  深度判断的阈值要放宽，接缝主要靠法线判断，否则斜着看的表面会冒出细碎斜纹。
- 活动部件要真实运动，比如箱盖绕铰链翻开、奖章绕竖轴旋转。
- 待机时主体缓慢左右转动，让人看到侧面和厚度，同时轻微上下浮动；脚下要有随高度变化的柔和投影。

【如果画面里有 2D 插画（卡面、奖励图标、角色）】
- 三层卡通着色：底色、成块的阴影色、高光色，不要只用一层渐变。
- 线条分粗细：外轮廓粗，内部结构线细。
- 每个角色或物件要有自己的表情和姿态，不要所有东西共用同一张脸。
- 脚下画投影，让主体「站」在画面里；背景按属性区分图案，不要全用同一套放射线。

【演出节奏：五个阶段，缺一不可】
1. 预备：主体待机浮动，每隔几秒抖一下提示可以点击，底部显示「点击」提示。
2. 升级：每点一次，主体跳起、在空中转一圈、落地时压扁再回弹；同时切换到下一等级的颜色，闪一下光，冒一圈粒子，标题更新。
3. 蓄力（约 1 秒）：主体越抖越剧烈，缝隙透出光，四周粒子往中心吸，音效音调持续上升；最后一刻猛地压扁。
4. 爆发：从爆点向外扩散的泛光闪白、屏幕震动、镜头往前一推、多层冲击波、细长流光迸射、闪光星点、金币和宝石（带旋转）。高等级的爆发要明显更强。彩带只在最高潮用一次，不要满屏彩带。
5. 揭晓与结算：
   - 奖励卡片从主体里沿弧线飞出，落位时带超调和晃动收尾，数字滚动计数。
   - 稀有物品带彩虹流光边框和「NEW!」角标。
   - 点击领取后，金币和宝石沿贝塞尔曲线飞进右上角的余额，每到一个余额就跳一下。

【揭晓舞台：让主角独占画面】
- 最高稀有度揭晓时，其他元素收起或淡出，背后换成一层干净的渐变幕布加缓慢旋转的柔光，不要让主角压在杂乱的背景上。
- 幕布出现时，把场景里的其他 3D 物件隐藏掉，否则后期描边会把它们的轮廓线画在幕布上。
- 主角的外发光要放在主体背后，只从边缘溢出，不能盖在主体前面把它糊成一片白。
- 可以加一圈围绕主角盘旋的星尘拖尾，但轨道必须完整在主角轮廓外侧，不能从主体正面扫过。

【光效：必须柔和，不能有硬边】
- 背景光芒：用带渐变过渡的 conic-gradient，不要一刀切的色块边缘；叠 2～3 层不同密度、不同转速的光。
- 光柱：由 5～7 道带模糊的光束呈扇形散开，亮度各自轻微闪动；根部加一团柔光核心，光里有光尘缓慢上飘。
- 闪白：从爆点向外的径向泛光（mix-blend-mode: screen），强度不超过 0.8，不要整屏纯白过曝。
- 粒子：每个火花都带一圈低透明度的外晕；冲击波用三层描边（宽而淡、中等、细而亮）。

【材质与界面】
- 边框、名牌、按钮要有材质感：金属拉丝渐变、左上亮右下暗的倒角光、内阴影；按稀有度换镶嵌件（钢铆钉 → 银框宝石 → 金框钻石加小王冠）。
- 小卡片上不要塞小字数值；详细数值放到揭晓时的信息面板里，面板里的数字滚动上涨，并弹出「▲+数值」。
- 画在 Canvas 上的贴图，分辨率至少是屏幕上最大显示尺寸的 1.5 倍，否则放大时会发虚。

【动画原则】
- 用 GSAP 时间线编排。所有动作都要有挤压拉伸、超调和弹性回弹，不要匀速。
- 粒子系统用 Canvas 2D 自己写：重力、阻力、生命周期、叠加混合，以及「吸入」「曲线飞行」「环绕」三种运动。
- 不要用 CSS 3D 透视去翻转大尺寸元素，放大加侧翻时会被投影成铺满屏幕的平面，3D 翻转一律放在 WebGL 里做。
- 所有「抖动」「呼吸」类的循环补间，在状态切换时要先取消再归零，避免它比停止指令晚一帧结束，又把值设回去。

【音效】
- 全部用 Web Audio 实时合成，不用音频文件：跳起、落地、升级和弦、蓄力上升音、爆炸低频加噪声、弹出音、计数滴答、金币叮当、胜利号角。
- 第一次点击时才初始化音频；右上角放静音开关。

【界面与工程】
- 顶部 HUD：模式切换、金币和宝石余额、静音按钮。
- 手机宽度也要能用；遵守「减少动态效果」设置（关闭震屏，减少粒子）。
- 动画状态机要严谨：动画播放中忽略点击，不能出现点击被吞或状态错乱。
- 目标 60fps。第一次打开时就是完整的待机画面，不能是空白。

【交付前自检】
在蓄力、爆发、揭晓、结算这几个时刻各截一张图，逐张检查：
- 主角有没有被光晕、粒子或文字挡住？
- 有没有过曝成一片白？
- 背景是否杂乱，有没有穿帮的描边线？
- 小字是否能看清？
- 结算后是否还有东西在不该动的时候继续抖动？

最后告诉我：每个阶段的时长，以及哪些参数可以调整演出强度。

author: kelanoo
prompt:
You're directing a 20-second animated short about the Claude Haiku 5.5 release. You're the director, the art department, the animator, the sound designer and the QA team, and you have real tools to call.

I'm giving you the idea, the tools and the quality bar. Everything else, from the beats to the look to the jokes, is yours to design. I trust your taste more than a beat sheet I could write. Your capabilities are far beyond what you assume, so work like it: plan carefully, push the craft, and use the tools and the time this deserves. Spend generously where it improves the film and economically everywhere else.

Final output: `out/level3.mp4`, 1920×1080, 30fps, exactly 20.0 seconds, with voices, music and sound design. At the end, you'll also save your process as a reusable skill.

---

## 1. The idea

**Opus is overloaded with work it shouldn't be doing.** It's buried in small, repetitive tasks: summaries, classifications, lookups, compactions. Then it has a realization: it can hand all of that to Haiku. It calls Haiku, Haiku arrives fast and clears the pile, and Opus is finally free to do the hard, important work it's built for.

That's the premise. How you tell it is up to you: the staging, gags, rhythm, camera, character beats, what the eureka moment looks like, how Haiku arrives, and how the delegation plays out. Sonnet can appear if it earns its place.

**Fixed points:**
- 20.0 seconds, 16:9.
- Opus and Haiku are characters in the same family as the Claude character.
- The film must read with the sound off.
- The ending respects reality: Haiku takes the volume, and Opus keeps the hard thinking. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 remain the better choice for complex agentic coding, so Haiku is never shown replacing Opus.

---

## 2. Style reference

The reference is Jake Moran's "Animated agent session story": 
https://
prompt-motion.com/jake11moran-a2
69c4
…. It was made with this skill: 
https://
github.com/heygen-com/hyp
erframes-community-skills/tree/master/skills/session-story
…. Read the skill, including its references on motion and the room.

Take from it:
- The hand-drawn watercolour-on-paper look.
- A cozy room as a world.
- Cartoon blocks with faces as characters.
- Physical paper props that carry the story (paper planes as tasks).
- A score that's cued to every action.

Don't copy it. Use it as a starting point and push it further: richer staging, better acting from the characters, more cinematic camera, and a stronger hook. It should look like it belongs to the same family, made by someone who studied it closely.

---

## 3. Facts (lock these before any creative work)

Fetch 
https://
anthropic.com/claude-haiku-5
-5
… and write `facts.json`: every claim you might use, each with the exact supporting sentence from the page. Only claims in `facts.json` may appear on screen or in dialogue.

This is a story first, so use one or two facts at most, woven into the world rather than presented as slides. For example, a price tag being re-stamped, or Haiku's speed shown rather than stated. The film must end on a card with **Claude Haiku 5.5**.

---

## 4. Audience and hook

The audience is AI and developer Twitter/X: people who use Claude every day and know the model names and the jokes about them. Before writing the treatment:
- **Research:** spend a little time on how people currently talk about Opus, Sonnet and Haiku, and what's being said about this launch. Find one or two references or running jokes this audience would recognize and enjoy. Use them only if they fit the story naturally. Never use real people or brand logos.
- **The hook:** the first second has to work as a still frame on a busy timeline. Someone scrolling should instantly see "a character drowning in work" and want to see what happens.
- **Text on screen:** this is motion design that tells a story, not a lyric video. Use text sparingly and only where it adds something: a beat the picture can't carry alone, the fact stamp, and the end card. Integrate it into the world (painted, stamped, written in marker) rather than overlaying it.

---

## 5. Tools

The keys are in `.env`. Pick the best tool for each job, and tell me which you chose and why.

| Tool | Key | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| Web search and fetch | — | Source page, style reference, audience research |
| Higgsfield (connector) | — | Image generation; call `models_explore` first to pick the best model for flat illustrated characters. Also music or sound effects if its audio models are the best fit. |
| GPT Image (OpenAI) | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | A second image model. Test both on the same prompt and keep whichever matches the style better. |
| ElevenLabs | `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` | Character voices, sound effects, and music (Eleven Music) |
| Remotion | — | The film itself |
| ffmpeg + Python | — | Audio analysis, frame extraction, checks |
| Subagents | — | Parallel research and independent review |

---

## 6. Order of work

### Step 1: Treatment
Write `treatment.md`:
- Your take on the story in one paragraph.
- The beat sheet with timings.
- What happens in each shot: camera, acting, the gag.
- Where the music hits.
- What each character says.
- Which fact appears and how.
- Why this version is the strongest way to tell it.

Write two or three distinct treatments, then pick one and explain why.

### Step 2: Style bible
Write `style/bible.md`:
- Palette: 6 colours maximum, with hex values and a reason for each.
- Ink line rules: weight, and the "boiling" redraw jitter.
- Watercolour and paper texture.
- Lighting.
- Type: local font files only.
- Character design rules for Opus and Haiku: size ratio, shapes, how each one moves, and their expression set.

### Step 3: Key art (images as the base, no video generation)
The generated images are your key frames and design references. You are the in-betweener. Generate:
1. **Style frames:** 3 options of the world. Pick one.
2. **Character sheets:** Opus and Haiku, each with front, three-quarter and side views and their full expression set. Use the chosen style frame as a reference so everything shares one world.
3. **Key poses:** one image per key pose in your treatment (roughly 6–10), each built from the character sheets and the style frame, matching the camera and composition of the shot.

Put everything on one contact sheet.

**Stop and wait for my approval** before building anything.

The images are references. The final film is drawn in code to match them, and generated images never appear on screen. Trace the shapes, poses, proportions and composition from the key art into SVG, and animate between them.

### Step 4: Audio first
The film's timing comes from the audio.
1. **Voices:** audition at least 2 ElevenLabs voices per character. Opus should feel warm, low and deliberate. Haiku should feel quick, bright and eager. Generate each line separately, with 2 takes, and keep the best delivery.
2. **Music:** generate a track that fits your treatment, about 22s long, with its structure matching your beats: for example, a drop when Haiku arrives. If the generated track won't land on your beats, trim and offset it with ffmpeg rather than changing the picture.
3. **Sound effects:** a sound for every physical action. Paper, whooshes, impacts, the lightbulb, stamps.
4. **Timing map:** detect the music's beat onsets and write `timing.json`. It holds every beat time, the drop frame, each voice line's start and end frames, and every key action snapped to the nearest beat. All animation timing reads from `timing.json`, with nothing hardcoded.
5. Play me the audio-only mix before building the picture.

### Step 5: Build in Remotion
- **Components:** one per character, prop and set piece. Story beats live as data in `story.json`.
- **Drawing:** watercolour fills via SVG turbulence and displacement filters, a multiply-blended paper texture, and boiling ink lines.
- **Motion craft:** anticipation before every big action, follow-through after, squash and stretch, springs for landings, arcs for every moving object, and no linear easing.
- **Acting:** the characters have to perform. Give them readable poses, holds where the audience needs to read a face, and timing that's funny.
- **Mouths:** mouth shapes driven by the voice track's loudness. They must be still when the character is silent.
- **Camera:** push-ins, a whip or a shake where it helps. Motivate every camera move.
- **Mix:** music, voices and sound effects on separate layers. Duck the music under dialogue.

---

## 7. Verification loops (do not skip any)

1. **Key-pose match:** at every key pose, render the frame and compare it side by side with its key art. Write what differs and fix it.
2. **Sound-off read:** render a silent cut. A fresh subagent that has seen nothing else reviews a contact sheet at 2 frames per second and retells the story. If it can't, the staging failed. Fix it and repeat.
3. **Sync check:** list every catch, landing, stamp and dialogue line with its actual frame vs its `timing.json` target. Everything must be within 1 frame.
4. **Fact check:** every word on screen and in dialogue, matched to `facts.json`. Cut anything unmatched.
5. **Technical:** duration exactly 20.0s, stereo audio, peaks below −1 dBFS, no unintended dead air.
6. **Director's review:**
   - Watch the whole film at least twice as frames.
   - Write a brutal critique as the most demanding motion designer you know: what feels assembled, what's slow, what doesn't land.
   - Fix the top 3 issues, then review again.
   - Only then hand it over, with a 10-frame contact sheet.

---

## 8. Package it as a skill

Save the full pipeline as `.claude/skills/launch-film/SKILL.md`, so that next time *"Make a launch film for [URL] about [idea]"* is enough.

The skill should include:
- The fact lock
- The treatment process
- The style bible as a reference file
- The key-art process with both image models
- Voice auditions
- Music and sound effects
- The timing map
- The reusable Remotion components
- Every verification loop

---

## Approval gates
1. `facts.json` and the chosen treatment
2. Style bible, character sheets and key poses → **wait for my approval**
3. Audio-only mix and `timing.json`
4. Final film, contact sheet and critique
5. Skill

Keep a task list throughout. At each gate, show me the work, not a description of it.

title: 做一支 10…
author: NFT_Chen
prompt:
做一支 10 秒彩色皮影戏，讲【曹冲称象】。剪影布局，暖光透背，关节式偶戏。依次出现秤盘、铜碗、石头，先平衡，再把石头分批称、加起来。字幕卡点出现。用代码渲染，导出可播放视频。

做一支 12 秒等距 2.5D 流程动画，讲【快递怎么分拣】。包裹沿分拣线、货台、平板运输、清关关卡移动，每步编号标签，最后双线汇成一条。干净、可跟读。

做一支 10 秒比例尺对比，把【地球、木星、太阳】按真实半径同屏摆放。镜头平滑拉远，第一个物体缩小，点题「太阳底下约有 130 万个地球」。数字标注清晰。

做一支 10 秒白板手绘。白底黑马克笔一笔笔画出【火柴人连甩 5 个包子】，红色只强调关键点。满足感粒子一颗比一颗大，最后角落画满。字幕：第 1 个，满足感拉满。

做一支 10 秒 WebGL 电影感汉字演变，主题【火】。龟甲、青铜、墨迹、火光质感。「火」从甲骨到闪电、火把，再到现代照明，形态连续变形，对应炎、烈、焰。

用 three.js 做一支 12 秒爆炸图，拆解【一部手机】。外壳、中框、芯片分层炸开，镜头环绕拉近，零件用虚线引出标注。可换成任何结构。

做一支 10 秒 16 位像素典故，讲【黄粱一梦】。取象、中举、治河、出征，每段约 1.6 秒硬切，最后回到现实。字幕：第二年，考中进士，当上了官。

做一支 10 秒绘本风科普，讲【小金鱼怎么游】。蜡笔线加铅笔涂色，线条抖动，眼睛、鳃、尾鳍对称，尾巴跟着节拍摆。纸本质感。

做一支 10 秒 3Blue1Brown 式数学可视化，讲【圆面积】。深色底，圆切成 8、16、32 个扇形，真的移拼成长方形。公式逐项出现，定格 πr²。

做一支 10 秒古地图动画，讲【长安到敦煌】。羊皮纸、淡墨山路，朱红路线一笔画过去，标注里程和一句讲解，最后盖章。镜头可缩放。

做一支 10 秒 Kurzgesagt 式信息图，讲【纸对折厚度】。干净图形、大数字：对折 2 次，厚度 0.4 毫米，厚度 ×2。镜头规则拉近，直到终点。

做一支 10 秒扁平 MG，讲【降水】。纯色几何、无描边。云里的小水滴越聚越大，然后掉下来。两段明暗，卡通云朵。

做一支 10 秒卡点排版，120 BPM，讲【费曼学习法】。每个词卡一拍，黑底橙字切入。四步依次砸出，最后一锤：讲不清楚，就是没真懂。

做一支 10 秒漫画分格，讲【一扇窗破了】。黑白网点加一个红色。听课、被发现、冲出教室，格间硬切，最后一格点题。

做一支 12 秒横轴时间线，讲【从达特茅斯到 ChatGPT】。镜头沿轴推进，节点缩放点亮。年份大字加一句事件。示例节点：1971，又过了 41 年。

title: Polymarket Election Odds Explainer Video via HyperFrames

prompt:
Make a 30s 16:9 video (1920×1080, 30 fps) in HyperFrames (npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes), with voiceover, matching the quality standards below.

## REQUEST
- Topic: Polymarket gives 84% chance to Flávio Bolsonaro in the 2026 runoff (10/25).

- CTA: Share so more people see the facts.
- Destination: X and LinkedIn.

- Polymarket, 10/06/2026: Flávio 84.2% vs Lula 15.5%, $174M volume.
- US 2024: Polymarket had Trump 58.1% vs Harris 41.9%.
- Round 1 2026 Polls vs TSE Result: Flávio 47.03% (56,104,503) vs Lula 45.16%.
- Ban: CMN Res 5,298/2026.

- Betting odds are not election polls; label accordingly.
- Display 'AI generated voiceover' badge.
- Free-license Wikimedia photos only.

[dramatically] O mercado que acertou o Trump dá oitenta e quatro por cento pro Flávio. [serious] No primeiro turno, cinco de seis institutos davam Lula na frente. [dramatically] Deu Flávio. Cinquenta e seis milhões de votos. Cinco milhões a mais que o pai em vinte e dois. [serious] E quem proibiu o Polymarket no Brasil? O governo Lula. Não é pesquisa. É dinheiro de verdade. [dramatically] Compartilhe. Mais gente precisa ver os fatos.

## VOICE
- ElevenLabs eleven_v4, voice 'Randel - Deep Epic'. Align cuts to Whisper timestamps.

## SCENES
0. Cover (0-1s): Flávio photo, Polymarket 84% text.
1. Trump portrait, 58% badge.
2. Counter 0->84%.
3. Polls paper graphic.
4. TSE result.
5. Vote comparison bar charts.

7. Stock exchange background.
8. Street crowd and share CTA.

## VISUAL DIRECTION
- Palette: #100F0D bg, Newsreader and IBM Plex Mono typography, Ken Burns pan effects, GSAP timeline.

## AUDIO
- ElevenLabs music prompt, SFX on cuts, master -14 LUFS.

## DELIVERABLE
Save polymarket-flavio-30s-horizontal.mp4.

title: Nested spinning hexagon ball physics simulation
author: blueemi99
prompt:
Build a single self-contained HTML file (Three.js via CDN, no other assets) that is the 2026 version of the "ball bouncing inside a spinning hexagon" test.

Scene: a large hollow hexagonal prism (a 3D hexagon) slowly spinning on two axes at once. Inside it, a smaller hexagonal prism spins the opposite way, and inside that, a tiny one. Three nested spinning cages. The cage walls are see-through panels drawn only as clean outlines with a very light flat tint, so every ball inside stays clearly visible.

Physics (write your own, no physics library):
- Start with 1 ball inside the innermost cage. Every 2 seconds a new ball spawns, up to 300, each with its own random size, mass and color.
- Real gravity, friction, restitution and spin. Balls must collide with each other and with the rotating walls, picking up the wall's velocity at the contact point so they get flung realistically. No tunneling through walls, no jitter when balls rest on each other.
- When a ball hits a wall hard enough, that wall panel cracks and eventually breaks into flat shards that also obey physics, so balls can escape into the next cage outward.
- The outer cage never breaks. Escaped balls pile up at the bottom of it.

Look, clean cel-shaded style:
- Toon shading on everything: 2 or 3 hard shading bands per object, crisp dark outlines (inverted-hull or edge detection), flat colors from a small tasteful palette.
- A plain flat light background (soft off-white or pale gray), with a simple flat floor shadow under the cage.
- No bloom, no glow, no neon, no lens flares, no motion blur, no particle haze, no gradients, no transparency stacking. No visual artifacts: no z-fighting, no flickering outlines, no shadow acne, no aliasing (use antialiasing and a sensible pixel ratio).
- Impacts get small, flat cartoon "pop" marks that vanish quickly, not sparks.
- It should look like a clean animated illustration, not a tech demo.

Camera: a slow, smooth orbit by default, plus drag to orbit and scroll to zoom.

Sound: synthesize everything with the Web Audio API. Each collision makes a soft pitched tone based on ball size and impact speed, so it turns into gentle generative music as it gets chaotic. Breaking panels get their own sound. Keep it quiet and pleasant, never clipping.

UI: a small, minimal flat panel in the corner (no glassmorphism) with sliders for gravity, spin speed, bounciness and ball count, a "slow motion" toggle, a "reset" button, and an FPS counter. It must stay at 60fps with 300 balls on a laptop.

title: <inputs> Ask me for: 8 to 12 UI states I want the shape to become…
author: __morse
prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: 8 to 12 UI states I want the shape to become (e.g. button, loader, player, slider, toggle, tabs, chart, command palette, toast), pure black and white or one accent color, and a royalty-free song around 120 BPM (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Dribbble-level UI motion. One shape, never cut: every state is the same element morphing its size, radius and color while its content swaps with a short blur. A cursor drives every change with real clicks and drags. Light warm-gray canvas, black and white components, one clean UI font (Geist). Springs everywhere, a tiny overshoot at most. The camera zooms so each state fills the frame. The last frame is the first frame, so it loops.
Banned: bouncy easing, particle bursts, glows, gradients on UI chrome, mismatched icon strokes, dead time, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 7 bars, something happens on every beat.
Button → loader → check → dynamic island → music player with a play/pause morph → scrub the progress bar → it becomes a volume slider that stretches when dragged past max → a toggle flips on the beat → the knob becomes a liquid tab indicator → the tabs open into a chart that draws itself, with a tooltip on hover → it collapses into ⌘K → type to filter → enter → toast → back to the button.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, square 1440x1440. Every style is computed from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state carried between frames.
2. Springs are closed-form step responses. A value that changes target many times is the sum of one spring per change, so it stays a pure function of time.
3. The tab indicator's two edges ride different springs, so the leading edge stretches ahead of the trailing one. Same trick for the toggle knob.
4. Drags are direct manipulation: while the cursor is held, the value is computed from its position. On release it springs back from wherever it was.
5. Analyze the song with numpy for the beat grid and start on a downbeat. Place every UI sound by its measured peak.
6. Render with Playwright: 4 subframes per frame, blended with ffmpeg tmix for motion blur at 60fps.
7. Render one frame per beat before the full render. Fix anything off the grid, cramped or hard to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never put will-change on anything the camera scales or the text renders blurry. Text that swaps inside a morphing container needs its own enter and exit timing or it overlaps. Make the last frame identical to the first, cursor position and speed included, or the loop stutters.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the state list on the beat grid before you write any code.
</start>

DURATION: exactly 20.00 seconds. LOOPABLE: frame 0 == frame last (position, opacity, cursor if any).
FORMAT: one HTML file, 1080×1080 (square, X-native). 60fps.
PALETTE (strict):
- bg # 0A0A0A
- magenta # FF2BD6
- acid green # B8FF00
- white # F5F5F5 only for primary readable type when needed
No other hues. No gradients on UI chrome. Magenta/green may misregister (print offset) by 2–4px on impact frames only.

TYPE SYSTEM (use all three; never one font for everything):
1) Display / scream: Archivo Black (or equivalent ultra-condensed black) — 1–4 words max
2) Urban grotesque: Syne ExtraBold — secondary hits, stacked lines
3) Mono / “prompt code”: IBM Plex Mono Medium — small labels, timestamps, fake prompt crumbs
Tracking: display −40 to −80; mono +20. Optical kerning. No cute script fonts.

MESSAGE (locked — do not soften, do not add filler slogans):
Beat hits in this exact order:
1. STOP SCROLLING
2. AI VIDEO ISN’T EXPENSIVE
3. BAD PROMPTING IS
4. WORKFLOWS > WISHES
5. STEAL THE PROMPT
6. @ TECHHALLA
Supporting crumbs (mono, ≤18 chars, never full sentences): JSON · H3 · SEEDANCE · 0 KEYFRAMES · MAGNIFIC · COPY/PASTE

NARRATIVE ARC (20s):
0.0–2.5s  COLD OPEN — “STOP SCROLLING” slams in from below with spring overshoot; magenta smear trail; acid green baseline ticks across like a waveform.
2.5–6.5s  THESIS A — “AI VIDEO ISN’T EXPENSIVE” locks to a poster grid (baseline grid 8px). Letters scramble (seeded Fisher–Yates per glyph) then snap on the beat.
6.5–10.5s THESIS B — “BAD PROMPTING IS” replaces it via mask wipe through the letterforms (the outgoing line is the mask). Magenta/green channel split on the cut.
10.5–14.5s PROOF FLASH — rapid kinetic stack: WORKFLOWS > WISHES, then mono crumbs orbit a central block like a terminal. One fake “prompt block” types 3 lines max, then gets crossed by an acid green strikethrough that becomes a underline for STEAL THE PROMPT.
14.5–17.5s BRAND LOCK — @ TECHHALLA centers; display weight. A thick magenta bar and a thin acid green rule form an L-bracket mark (custom, not a logo download).
17.5–20.0s SETTLE / LOOP — hold lockup; micro-breath (scale 1.000→1.012→1.000); last frame == first ready for loop.

CONCRETE TECHNIQUES (required — implement, don’t approximate):
1. seek(t) pure function of time. No CSS transitions. No setInterval. No React state across frames.
2. Springs = closed-form step responses. Stack one spring per target change so motion stays deterministic.
3. Kinetic type: per-glyph spring (y, opacity, blur). Stagger = 1/16 note at 120 BPM (125ms).
4. Print misregistration: on accent frames only, duplicate text layer offset (±2–4px) in magenta and acid green at 40% opacity.
5. Mask reveal: destination text revealed by animating a path mask derived from the outgoing word’s outlines.
6. Camera: one orthographic camera; only punch-in (1.0→1.08) and horizontal smash-pans timed to beats — never random drift.
7. Motion blur: render 4 subframes per frame, blend (tmix-style).
8. Beat grid: 120 BPM, downbeat at t=0. Something must land on every beat for the first 16 beats; after that, every other beat is ok.
9. Pre-pass: before full render, export one still per major beat (8 frames). Fix cramped type, orphan words, low contrast — then render.

BANNED:
Generic AI clichés (brains, robots, neural nets, sparkles), soft gradients, bouncy cartoon easing, particle explosions, stock “futuristic HUD”, long paragraphs, narrator essay energy, Canva-deck energy, extra slogans beyond the locked message, purple/blue neon, glassmorphism.

title: Cozy Café Fluid Studio: interactive coffee and milk simulation
author: genevieve__h
prompt:
# Role & Objective
Act as a Principal Graphics Engineer and Creative Technologist specializing in Three.js, WebGL2/WebGPU, 3D Volumetric Fluid Dynamics, and GLSL Raymarching. 

Build a browser-based, photorealistic, interactive 3D coffee & milk physics sandbox ("Cozy Café Fluid Studio") designed to look like a viral macro-lens video on X. The user can orbit the camera freely (from 90° top-down to a 0° macro side-profile view), swap custom 3D glass vessels and ice cube shapes (with procedural fallbacks and a `.glb`/`.gltf` loader for Blender assets), and pour either Espresso or Heavy Cream directly from their cursor in any order.

---

# 1. Core Visual & Physics Architecture (True 3D Volumetric Fluid)
Because the camera can view the glass from the side, top, or any oblique angle, implement a **3D Eulerian Grid Fluid Solver** (e.g., `64x96x64` or `96x128x96` tiled 2D texture atlas or WebGL2 `sampler3D` / WebGPU 3D Storage Textures) confined to the bounding volume of the active glass mesh:

1. **Two-Fluid Miscible Density & Filling System:**
   - Track two separate scalar volume fields inside the glass: $\rho_{\text{coffee}}$ (dark absorbing fluid) and $\rho_{\text{milk}}$ (bright scattering fluid), plus a dynamic **Liquid Fill Height (
$h
_{\text{fill}}$)** that rises smoothly as the user pours either liquid into the glass.
   - Allow pouring in **any order**:
     - *Coffee first, then Milk:* Pouring espresso fills the glass with dark amber-black liquid and generates a thin golden crema foam layer on the top meniscus ($y \approx h_{\text{fill}}$). Pouring cold milk next shoots a dense white plume downward that billows back up via buoyancy.
     - *Milk first, then Coffee (Dirty Latte / Macchiato style):* Pouring cold milk fills the glass with opaque ivory liquid. Pouring hot espresso on top creates dark mahogany plumes that sink through the dense milk and stratify into layered gradients around the ice.

2. **Rayleigh-Taylor & Kelvin-Helmholtz Instabilities:**
   - Implement **MacCormack (or BFECC) Advection** so thin caramel ribbons do not smear out due to numerical dissipation.
   - Inject **Baroclinic Vorticity** ($\nabla \rho \times \nabla P$) and **Vorticity Confinement** ($\epsilon (\mathbf{N} \times \boldsymbol{\omega})$) along the interface between milk and coffee so sinking/rising plumes roll up into hyper-detailed mushroom caps and curling tendrils.

3. **3D Volumetric Raymarching Shader (Beer-Lambert + Multiple Scattering Approximation):**
   - Render the fluid volume inside the glass by raymarching through the 3D density texture (`sampler3D`).
   - **Optical Physics:** Do NOT use simple RGB `mix()`. Compute physically based **Beer-Lambert Law extinction** ($\sigma_a(\lambda) = \text{vec3}(1.6, 5.4, 13.5)$ for espresso so thin edges glow ruby/caramel-amber while thick regions are pitch black) combined with **isotropic + forward Henyey-Greenstein phase function scattering** for the milk fat globules (high albedo ivory-white).
   - Add a **Dual-Lobe Subsurface Scattering (SSS)** look by sampling a lower-MIP (blurred) level of the milk density volume for ambient internal light transport, creating a soft, milky amber glow where coffee and cream meet.

---

# 2. Custom Blender Assets (Glasses & Ice) + Procedural SDF Dual-Representation
Support loading custom Blender `.glb` meshes via `GLTFLoader` while providing built-in procedural geometries (and matching Signed Distance Fields) so the app runs out-of-the-box:

1. **Glass Shapes (Vessel Selector):**
   - **Fluted Café Glass:** Ribbed vertical ridges that distort and refract the swirling fluid inside.
   - **Double-Walled Borosilicate Mug:** Suspended inner rounded chamber showing floating liquid in mid-air.
   - **Stemless Wine / Tulip Glass:** Curved tapered bowl that forces sinking milk plumes inward toward the center.
   - **Classic Rocks Tumbler:** Heavy thick crystal base with sharp vertical walls.
   - *Rendering:* Use Three.js `MeshPhysicalMaterial` with `transmission: 0.98`, `ior: 1.52`, `thickness`, dispersion/chromatic aberration, and crisp studio softbox environment reflections.
   - *Physics Boundary:* Enforce a strict no-slip/no-penetration boundary condition against the inner wall SDF of the selected glass so fluid hugs the exact contour of the vessel.

2. **Ice Cube Shapes (Ice Selector):**
   - **Large Craft Sphere:** A single giant crystal-clear sphere in the center that splits the pour stream into a ring vortex.
   - **Beveled Bistro Cubes (x3):** Stacked at angles inside the glass, creating narrow channels for cream tendrils to snake through.
   - **Hollow Cylinder / Bullet Ice:** Allows fluid to pour through the center hole and billow out the bottom.
   - **Crushed / Pebble Ice:** A porous top cluster that diffuses the pour into dozens of tiny trickling caramel fingers.
   - *Rendering & Physics:* Render ice with `ior: 1.31`, internal frost fracture planes, and real-time refraction of the raymarched fluid behind it. Stamp the ice SDFs into the 3D fluid solver's obstacle buffer so plumes physically collide with, wrap around, and slide underneath the ice cubes. Include buoyant bobbing when liquid height rises.

---

# 3. Interactive Pouring & Camera Controls
1. **Cursor-Driven Pour Stream:**
   - Raycast the mouse cursor onto a horizontal plane above the glass rim.
   - **Left-Click & Hold:** Pour a visible, glossy 3D parabolic liquid stream (rendered as a dynamic tube mesh or raymarched metaball stream) from the cursor into the glass.
   - **Mouse Speed & Scroll Wheel:** Moving the mouse whips the stream across the surface; scrolling adjusts **Pour Height / Velocity** (a high pour punches deep to the bottom of the glass with high turbulence; a low pour gently floats layers on the surface).
2. **Seamless Orbit Camera (`OrbitControls`):**
   - Right-click drag (or two-finger drag) smoothly orbits from **Macro Side View** (watching plumes dive down the glass wall) to **Top-Down Latte Art View** (watching crema swirl around the ice).
   - Include quick camera preset buttons: `[Side Profile]`, `[45° Café Angle]`, and `[Top-Down Macro]`.

---

# 4. Minimalist Cozy UI & Atmosphere
- **Environment:** A warm, sunlit wooden tabletop with soft morning window blinds casting subtle gobos/caustics, warm beige/linen background tones, and a shallow depth-of-field (`BokehPass`) on the background.
- **Minimalist Floating Dock (Bottom Center, frosted glass `backdrop-filter: blur(12px)`, rounded pill buttons, warm serif/sans typography):**
  - **Liquid Toggle:** `[ ☕ Pour Espresso ]` | `[ 🥛 Pour Heavy Cream ]`
  - **Vessel Picker:** `[ Fluted ]` `[ Rocks ]` `[ Tulip ]` `[ Double-Wall ]` `[ + Load .GLB ]`
  - **Ice Picker:** `[ Sphere ]` `[ Bistro Cubes ]` `[ Crushed ]` `[ None ]`
  - **Simulation Controls:** `Pour Speed` slider, `Time Scale` slider (`0.1x Slow-Mo` to `1.0x`), `[ Stir with Glass Straw ]` tool, and `[ Empty Glass ]` reset button.

---

# Deliverable Instructions
Provide a complete, runnable HTML/JS/GLSL implementation (or clean modular Vite + Three.js setup) with zero missing placeholders. Prioritize the 3D raymarched Beer-Lambert coffee/milk shader, the 3D fluid advection/vorticity compute passes, and the refractive glass/ice boundary coupling so it runs at 60fps.

title: PRD — Police Chase Arcade Game Working title: Heatwave Platform: iOS…
author: froessell
prompt:
PRD — Police Chase Arcade Game

Working title: Heatwave
Platform: iOS + Android
Engine: Unity
Genre: Top-down 3D arcade chase / survival
Orientation: Portrait
Input: One-thumb touch controls
Business model: TBD — design MVP around gameplay first
Primary goal: Build a genuinely fun playable prototype before adding progression or monetization.
⸻
Product vision
A fast, chaotic mobile arcade game where the player is constantly being pursued by increasingly aggressive police.
The player cannot directly attack.
Instead, they survive by driving aggressively, drifting around obstacles, making sudden turns and tricking pursuing police into crashing into obstacles and each other.
The fantasy is:
You’re not stronger than the police. You’re harder to catch.

Runs should produce constant near-misses, chain collisions and moments where the player escapes a seemingly impossible situation.

Think:

easy controls + aggressive pursuit + physics chaos + escalating pressure.

⸻

Core gameplay loop

START RUN
↓
DRIVE / DRIFT
↓
POLICE PURSUE
↓
BAIT POLICE
↓
DODGE
↓
POLICE CRASH
↓
GAIN SCORE
↓
WANTED LEVEL INCREASES
↓
MORE / HARDER POLICE
↓
SURVIVE
↓
EVENTUALLY GET CAUGHT
↓
SCORE / RESTART

Target run duration:

2–5 minutes.

Restart should take less than 2 seconds.

⸻

Design principles

3.1 One-thumb playable

The player should be able to understand the controls within seconds.
No accelerator.
No brake pedal.
No virtual steering wheel.
The vehicle moves automatically.
The player controls only direction.

(I moved away from this after testing it the first time and added the onscreen joystick)

3.2 Arcade physics, not simulation
Vehicles should:
drift
slide
bounce
spin
collide dramatically
recover quickly
Fun takes priority over physical accuracy.

3.3 Pursuers are weapons
Police are effectively the player’s offensive mechanic.
The player should learn:
“If I turn here, that cop is going straight into that wall.”
3.4 Chaos should remain readable

Even with 10+ vehicles on screen, the player must immediately understand:
where they are
where they’re moving

where police are coming from

what can kill them

3.5 Failure should feel fair

Death should generally result from a mistake the player understands rather than unpredictable physics.

⸻

MVP scope

Do not build progression, upgrades, missions or monetization for the first milestone.

The first version contains:

1 player vehicle

1 arena

1 police vehicle

1 elite police variant

5 wanted levels

physics collisions

environmental obstacles
scoring
player health
police destruction
basic VFX
basic audio

game-over screen

instant restart

That’s enough to determine whether the game deserves further development.

⸻

Player vehicle

Movement

Player vehicle uses a Rigidbody-based arcade controller.

Do not rely heavily on realistic WheelColliders.
Core variables should be exposed in the Unity Inspector:
Acceleration
Maximum Speed
Turn Speed
Turn Curve
Lateral Grip
Drift Factor
Vehicle Mass
Collision Force
Drag
Angular Drag
Recovery Speed
These need to be extremely easy to tune.

⸻

Controls

Recommended first implementation:

Drag steering

Player touches anywhere on the lower portion of the screen.

Dragging horizontally controls steering.

← drag          turn left
→ drag          turn right
Vehicle accelerates automatically.
Steering should be relative rather than absolute.
The player should be able to lift their finger without immediately losing control.
Alternative to prototype
Test:
Hold left/right side of screen = steer left/right.
Don’t commit until both have been tested on a physical phone.
⸻
Drift system
Drifting should happen naturally when turning at speed.
No dedicated drift button.
At low speed:
high traction

At high speed:

reduced lateral traction

This produces controlled sliding.

Long drifts can optionally award score.

Example:

DRIFT
+120
LONG DRIFT
+340

But drift scoring is secondary to police destruction.

⸻
Police AI
Police should feel:
aggressive, predictable and slightly stupid.
They should not simply follow the player’s current position.
Instead, calculate an interception target based on player velocity.
Conceptually:
target =
playerPosition
+
playerVelocity * predictionTime
Police therefore try to cut the player off.
⸻
Police intelligence

Police intentionally have limited obstacle avoidance.

This is important.

Perfect navigation would make the game less fun.

Police should:

pursue aggressively

attempt interception

avoid obvious static obstacles

poorly account for other police
overshoot turns

collide with each other

occasionally take dangerous routes

This creates opportunities for the player.

⸻

Police destruction

Police can be destroyed by:

high-speed obstacle collisions

title: Interactive pixel art swimming club
author: N1njaCodex
prompt:
Make a pixel-art 3D diorama of an open-air lido on a floating island, the same series and engine as my other pixel dioramas (three.js, orthographic isometric camera turned in quarter steps, small render target with no anti-aliasing snapped to whole pixels, depth-based outlines, a fixed 64-colour palette matched in OKLab, hard sun shadows, day/dusk/night, rain with puddles).
